newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq hopes oil prize will lift U.N. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iraq hopes oil prize will lift U.N. sanctions.

text.p: Iraq's oilfield potential has become one of Baghdad's strongest cards in its diplomatic drive to get the United Nations to lift sanctions imposed after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, analysts said on Wednesday.

Iraq has courted key U.N. Security Council members with offers of production rights in the world's second largest reserves of oil, banking that economic self-interest will ease opposition to blanket sanctions and rejuvenate the country's battered and investment-starved oil sector, they said.

"Iraq would like to get out of the isolation and to invite foreign companies to come and develop oilfields...They need that both financially and politically. Iraq needs to have as many contracts as possible," said Fadhil Chalabi, executive director of the Centre for Global Energy Studies.
Baghdad needs to prove to the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) that it has destroyed its weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations considers lifting sanctions completely.
Iraqi officials this month have played up multi-billion dollar oilfield negotiations with permanent Security Council members Russia, China, France and Group of Seven member Italy.

This coincides with an effort by Baghdad to get the United Nations to allow Iraq to export more of its oil under the limited "oil-for-food" deal which has allowed Iraq since December last year to export $1 billion of its crude every 90 days.

Baghdad's chief U.N. oil negotiator Abdul Amir al-Anbari on Tuesday called on the United Nations to double the financial ceiling for Iraq's humanitarian oil sales when the deal comes up for renewal in June. U.N. diplomats say the deal will be renewed unchanged.
Iraqi oil officials have also been upbeat that more foreign firms would commit themselves this year to developing Iraq's oilfields as soon as sanctions were lifted.

Three Russian firms led by LUKoil last month signed a contract to develop Iraq's West Qurna field, a project that could see output from the giant reservoir reach a million barrels per day (bpd) in four to six years.

Russian officials have said that only feasibility and financing work would begin before sanctions ended though under the terms of the deal the bill for this work would run as high as $300 million while sanctions remained in place.
"West Qurna is a done deal. Russia has said it will remain within the letter of the sanctions law but the Iraqis have secured a definite development deal," a Gulf-based analyst said.

Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, after talks last week in Rome with Italian energy group ENI, said subsidiary Agip was close to a $2 billion investment deal to develop the 300,000 bpd capacity Nasiriya field.
Iraq is also in negotiations that could see Chinese firms develop its 80,000 bpd al-Ahdab and 250,000 bpd Halfaya fields. A deal has already been agreed in principle for al-Ahdab.

But chances Baghdad might secure final signatures on these contracts before sanctions end look slim. ENI has declined comment on its talks with Rasheed but officials say privately no final contract will emerge before sanctions are lifted.

State Chinese National Petroleum Corp said it had maintained contacts with Baghdad but would not proceed until trade curbs are lifted. CNPC said it had received a number of invitations to visit Iraq but had no immediate plans for the trip.
France's Total SA and Elf Aquitaine both have contracts pending for the 500,000 bpd Nahr Umr and 300,000 bpd Majnoon fields once sanctions are lifted.
Again, final agreement depends on an end to sanctions.

"There is no way we could sign these agreements unless there is a positive political atmosphere. The situation is improving gradually in Iraq's favour. There is a clear appreciation of Iraq's position now which is encouraging the signing of these strategic agreements," Rasheed told the Middle East Economic Survey (MEES) weekly newsletter.

Iraqi oil plans envisage attracting $15 billion under foreign production sharing agreements over ten years after sanctions are lifted, helping to boost output capacity to six million bpd from a current 2.5 million bpd.
